blocks.content: A cache has a fixed size. When it fills up and a new entry needs space, the eviction policy decides which existing entry gets removed. Choosing the right policy directly affects your cache hit rate.
Eviction is space-driven triggered when the cache is full. TTL expiry is time-driven triggered by age. Both happen independently. A cache uses both simultaneously.
1. Least Recently Used (LRU)

Tracks when each entry was last accessed. When the cache is full, the entry that hasn't been read or written for the longest time gets evicted. The assumption: if you haven't touched it recently, you probably won't soon.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129486-192047080.png
Cache is already full and a new entry E needs to be inserted. Each existing item has a last access time which tells when it was last used.
A was used 10 seconds ago, B 2 seconds ago, D 8 seconds ago, and C 45 seconds ago.
C is the oldest in terms of last access, meaning it has not been used for the longest time.
LRU (Least Recently Used) assumes that data not used recently is least likely to be used again soon.
So C is selected for eviction. C is removed from cache to free space.
Now E is inserted into the cache. After this, cache contains A, B, D, and E.
This keeps frequently and recently used data in cache while removing stale usage patterns.
How it's implemented ( doubly linked list + hashmap )
blocks.text: How it's implemented ( doubly linked list + hashmap )

blocks.content: LRU needs O(1) get and O(1) update of access order. A hashmap handles O(1) lookup. A doubly linked list maintains order the head is most recently used, the tail is least recently used. On every access, move that node to the head.
Use when: general-purpose caching user data, sessions, API responses. The Redis default (allkeys-lru) and the right choice for 80% of use cases.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279688855-501302996.png
blocks.alt: A hashmap maps keys to nodes while a doubly linked list keeps them ordered from most to least recently used

blocks.content: 2. Least Frequently Used (LFU)
Tracks how many times each entry has been accessed across its lifetime in the cache. The entry with the lowest total access count gets evicted. Frequency matters more than recency.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129487-896243514.png
Cache is full and a new entry E new entry needs to be inserted.
Each item has total access count like A 920 hits, B 445 hits, D 211 hits, and C 3 hits evict.
C 3 hits evict has the fewest total accesses, meaning it is least frequently used.
LFU (Least Frequently Used) keeps highly accessed data and removes rarely used data.
So C is selected for eviction. C is removed from cache to free space.
Now E new entry is inserted into cache. After this, cache keeps A, B, D because they have higher usage. C evicted fewest total accesses. A, B, D stay.
How it's implemented ( min-heap or frequency buckets )
blocks.text: How it's implemented ( min-heap or frequency buckets )

blocks.content: LFU tracks a count per key and needs to quickly find the minimum-frequency key. The efficient approach: a hashmap of key → (value, freq), plus a hashmap of freq → set of keys at that frequency, plus a minFreq pointer.
Use when: your access pattern has a clear hot tier product pages, popular posts, config values accessed thousands of times vs long-tail data. Redisallkeys-lfuis good for CDN-like workloads.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129488-678564248.png
blocks.alt: How it's implemented  min-heap or frequency buckets

blocks.content: 3. First In First Out
The simplest possible policy. Tracks only insertion order. The entry that was added to the cache first gets evicted first regardless of how many times it's been accessed since.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129488-539974780.png
Cache is full and a new entry E new entry needs to be inserted.
Items were inserted in order: A inserted 1st evict, B inserted 2nd, C inserted 3rd, D inserted 4th.
FIFO (First In First Out) removes the oldest inserted item.
Since A inserted 1st evict came first, it is selected for removal.
Even if A is frequently used, FIFO does not consider usage. So A is evicted from cache. Now E new entry takes its place.
Final result: A evicted even if hottest key while B, C, D remain.
Use when: data has a natural freshness window and all entries expire equally rate limit windows, sliding time buckets, or job queues where oldest = least relevant. Not for general-purpose caching.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129488-972043857.png
4. LRU vs LFU  the key trade-off
These two are the most important to understand deeply since they're the real choice in practice.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129489-961251678.png
blocks.alt: LRU vs LFU the key trade-off

blocks.content: LRU: recency wins
LRU looks at recent usage, not total usage.
Items: A 1s, B 3s, C 8s, D 60s ← out
D 60s ← out is removed because it was not used for the longest time. Even if D had very high usage earlier, it still gets evicted.
A is kept just because it was used recently, even if it may never be used again.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279691815-444938874.png
blocks.alt: LRU example: item D was used 60 seconds ago, the longest gap, so it is evicted

blocks.content: LFU: frequency wins
LFU looks at total number of accesses, not recent usage.
Items: A 9400, B 2200, C 2 ← out
C 2 ← out is removed because it has the lowest number of hits. Even if C was accessed recently, it still gets evicted.
A is kept because it has very high usage, even if it was last used long ago.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129489-297076852.png
